answer_text:
Assume the interval is nondegenerate, i.e. \(a<b\).

Consider the integrable step function

\[
f(t)=
\begin{cases}
1, & a\le t<\frac{a+b}{2},\\[2mm]
-1, & \frac{a+b}{2}\le t\le b.
\end{cases}
\]

Then

\[
\int_a^b f(t)\,dt
=
\int_a^{\frac{a+b}{2}} 1\,dt
+
\int_{\frac{a+b}{2}}^b (-1)\,dt
=
\frac{b-a}{2}-\frac{b-a}{2}
=
0.
\]

Also,

\[
\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt
=
\int_a^b 1\,dt
=
b-a>0.
\]

If a constant \(C\) satisfied

\[
\left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\right|
\ge
C\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt
\]

for every integrable \(f\), then applying it to the above \(f\) would give

\[
0 \ge C(b-a).
\]

Since \(b-a>0\), this is impossible if \(C>0\). Therefore no positive universal constant \(C\) exists.

On the other hand, \(C=0\) always works because the left-hand side is nonnegative. Thus the largest admissible nonnegative constant is \(0\).

\[
\boxed{\text{No positive constant exists; the largest such nonnegative constant is } C=0.}
\]
